source.title: Double Descent Meets Out-of-Distribution Detection: Theoretical Insights and Empirical Analysis on the role of model complexity
source.authors: Mouïn Ben Ammar; David Brellmann; Arturo Mendoza; A. Manzanera; Gianni Franchi

record.file_problem: The paper and appendices are present. Some equations and tables are flattened in the extraction, but the relevant findings are readable.
record.tranche_reason: It varies model width and reports test accuracy, following the cited width-scaling setup from Nakkiran et al.; it also tests double descent for OOD measures.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own width-sweep results for ID test accuracy and OOD measures, plus theoretical bounds and a random-feature experiment. It also reports a noiseless comparison and depth-wise results. Cited findings from other work are not recorded. Specific values used only to set hyperparameters are not results.
record.test_reason: It replicates Nakkiran et al.'s width sweep with 20% label noise and reports ID test accuracy versus width for CNN, ResNet-18/34, ViT and Swin. It adds a noiseless control and a least-squares and random-feature analysis of ID risk. Most of the paper concerns OOD detection AUC, which is a different construct from test error.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that double descent appears in post-hoc OOD detection across architectures. They also show theoretically that both ID and OOD risks peak at the interpolation threshold for least-squares classifiers on Gaussian data. They find overparameterization is not uniformly better, and propose the NC1 ratio as an indicator of when larger models detect OOD better.
record.recipe_differences: The paper follows Nakkiran et al.'s width-scaling setup, including noisy labels and test accuracy, but focuses on OOD detection, uses several architectures and detectors, and adds theoretical and representation analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effect varies with architecture, OOD method family, dataset, label noise, and scaling dimension (width versus depth). The interpolation threshold is not always consistent across OOD datasets or techniques.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-hoc OOD detection AUC (logit-based and hybrid detectors) and the theoretical OOD risk follow a double-descent curve over width and depth. Feature-based detectors sometimes do not. The noiseless setting shows a plateau. Depth-wise best under- and overparameterized models are comparable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: OOD detection performance of post-hoc detectors shows double descent with model capacity, peaking in error at the interpolation threshold.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2025 (39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)
record.problems: Many empirical curves are available only as figures without exact values in the text. Some feature-based-method cases lack double descent, but the cited passage does not identify each case. The theoretical analysis uses simplified Gaussian and least-squares settings. Experiments use five seeds for the general setup, but the noiseless appendix passage does not state uncertainty details.
record.rows_left_out: Did not extract individual figure-only AUC curves for each detector, architecture, and OOD dataset from Figures 2, 4–17, 19, and 23–24; the main text reports grouped outcomes, and the detailed plots would exceed the useful row budget. Also omitted Table 1 and Appendix Table 2 endpoint AUC comparisons because they compare under- and overparameterized endpoints rather than report the full curve.

untested.parts: Only the width axis with 20% label noise on CIFAR; no other noise levels and no non-image tasks.
No sweep of test error over epochs.
Only least-squares, random-feature and deep vision models; no kernels, trees or other model classes.
Effective model complexity is only mentioned in passing; peak location is not predicted across axes.
Regularization, variance levels and multiple peaks are not tested; only noisy versus noiseless labels.

missing.what: Random ReLU feature model ID MSE test loss versus width, peaking near the interpolation threshold (width about 1000).
ResNet-34 ID accuracy versus width on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. The threshold is at k=8, versus k=10 for ResNet-18.
ResNet-18 ID accuracy versus width with CIFAR-100 as ID.
Depth-wise ID test accuracy double descent in ResNet-like models with width fixed at 10.
Noiseless ResNet-18 max accuracy is 94.48%, versus 83.40% with noise.

record.verdict_notes: The originals are Nakkiran et al. and Belkin et al. 2019. The theory extends Belkin et al. 2020, which is not an original source. Most rows concern OOD detection and were moved to fits_no_version. Transformers never reach full interpolation, which weakens their bearing on V1.

versions.untested_parts: Tests width-wise ID test accuracy for several architectures, but not the claim's full range of deep-network settings.
Training duration is specified, but test error is not swept over epochs.
Does not vary training sample size near the interpolation threshold.
Tests selected Gaussian/least-squares, random-feature, and neural-network settings, not a broad survey of model classes.
Discusses effective model complexity and threshold variation, but does not test whether one measured complexity quantity predicts peak location across size, epochs, and samples.
Compares noisy-label and noiseless settings. Does not test variance levels, multiple/triple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization.
Does not re-count parameters using an appropriate effective parameter measure or test whether that yields an ordinary U-shape.
